questions.question: A policyholder minimises expected monetary cost. Reporting gives reimbursement 100 now, incurs a separate processing fee 20 now, and adds future premiums with present value 90. No other consequences apply. Which decision and reason are correct?
options: Report, because reimbursement 100 exceeds the future premium cost 90.
Report, because the fee 20 reduces the future premium cost from 90 to 70.
Be indifferent, because the accident loss itself is unchanged by reporting.
Suppress, because total reporting cost 110 exceeds reimbursement 100.

questions.question: Reporting leads to future premium expected present value A; not reporting leads to B, with $A,B\ge 0$. Current reimbursement is $R>0$. Which formula gives the future incremental cost caused by reporting for every admissible A,B,R?
A simple hunger-for-bonus rule compares reimbursement R with expected discounted extra premiums V. Which decision objective makes that monetary comparison the stated decision rule?
options: Minimising only the number of submitted reports.
Minimising expected monetary costs over the chosen horizon.
Maximising current reimbursement while ignoring future premiums.
Minimising the current premium already paid.

questions.question: Some policyholders pay small accident losses themselves to avoid report-triggered premium increases. The physical accidents have already occurred. What does this behaviour change directly in the insurer records?
options: The physical accident frequency must fall in the same proportion as reported frequency.
The recorded severity distribution must remain unchanged when small claims are suppressed.
Reported experience may understate actual accident experience.
The contractual coverage threshold automatically rises when claims are suppressed.

questions.question: A contract reimburses losses above its contractual coverage threshold. Separately, the policyholder may suppress a reimbursable claim to avoid future premium increases. Must this behavioural reporting threshold equal the contractual threshold?
options: No; future premium incentives can suppress covered claims.
Yes; every covered claim must be reported under the cost rule.
Yes; future experience rating changes the contract threshold itself.
No; only losses outside coverage can ever be suppressed.

questions.question: A covered claim gives reimbursement 100 and exactly 100 of expected discounted extra premiums if reported. No other costs or benefits apply, and no tie-breaking rule is specified. What does expected-cost minimisation imply?
options: Reporting is strictly cheaper because reimbursement is positive.
Reporting and non-reporting have equal expected cost.
Non-reporting is strictly cheaper because future premiums rise.
The policyholder must split the claim amount equally.

questions.question: Reporting gives reimbursement 35 now and an additional premium of 40 one year later. The discount factor to that date is 0.8, with no other consequences. Under expected-cost minimisation, what is the reporting advantage?

Four actual covered losses are 10, 20, 100 and 200. A reporting incentive suppresses the two amounts below 50, while the other two are reported. What is the mean amount in the insurer reported-loss sample?

Two current history states charge the same premium today but lead to different future price paths after a report. Reimbursement is the same for both policyholders. Must their hunger-for-bonus decisions agree?
options: Yes; the current price alone determines the reporting threshold.
Yes; equal reimbursement removes every future consideration.
No; the contract must reimburse different amounts in the two states.
No; equal current prices need not give equal future increments.

questions.question: A policyholder has reached the end of all possible renewals. Reporting a covered claim gives positive reimbursement R and has no current fees or future premium effects. What does expected monetary-cost minimisation favour?
options: Reporting, because the future premium increment is zero.
Suppressing, because every report necessarily destroys a future bonus.
Indifference, because there are no future premiums.
Suppressing, because the current premium cannot be refunded.

questions.question: An accident causes damage X with partial reimbursement $0<R<X$ if reported. Reporting adds future cost $V\ge 0$, and all other costs are shared. Which amounts should be compared under the monetary reporting rule for every such X,R,V?
options: Compare X with V, because all damage is refunded on reporting.
Compare R with V, because unreimbursed damage is common.
Compare X with R, while excluding future premiums.
Compare X+R with V, counting both damage and compensation.

questions.question: Reporting will reimburse 100 at the end of year 2 and add 60 to premiums at the end of year 1. The annual discount factor is 0.8, with no other reporting costs or benefits. What is the present-value reporting advantage under monetary-cost minimisation?

Reporting reimburses 50 now. It adds 100 to next year's premium only if the policy renews, which has probability 0.5. The one-year discount factor is 0.9. What is the expected present future cost of reporting?

One claim is already reported. Next premium would have been 100 with no reports; it is 180 with the existing report and 190 if a second claim is reported. The second claim reimburses 60 now. Ignoring discounting and other effects, what incremental saving comes from the second report?

A reporting model has true mean annual accident frequency $\lambda>0$ and independent report probability $p\in(0,1]$ per accident, so mean reported frequency is $m=p\lambda$. The insurer observes m=0.4 but does not know p. Is the accident frequency identified?
options: Yes; the observed frequency always equals the accident frequency.
Yes; one observed mean determines both positive parameters.
No; different accident and reporting rates can give the same m.
No; reported frequency must exceed accident frequency.

questions.question: Reporting gives reimbursement 80 and raises next-year premium by 50 in two possible contracts, with no discounting. In contract A no later increments occur; in contract B a further 100 increase occurs in year 2. Under two-year monetary-cost minimisation, does the common next-year increase determine the decision?
options: Yes; both favour reporting because 80 exceeds 50.
No; A favours reporting whereas B favours suppression.
Yes; both favour suppression because any premium increase is decisive.
No; their current reimbursements must actually differ.

questions.question: Two covered accidents each reimburse 60. Future premium increases are 0 if neither is reported, 100 if exactly one is reported, and 110 if both are reported. Ignore discounting and other effects. Although each claim alone is unattractive, which joint report choice minimises total monetary cost?
options: Report neither, applying the isolated one-claim rule twice.
Report exactly one, because the second report adds 10 more premium.
Either choice is tied because both claims have the same amount.
Report both, as 120 reimbursed exceeds the joint increase of 110.

questions.question: Reporting reimburses 15 now and adds premiums 10 at year 1 and 20 at year 2. A common annual discount factor is $\delta\in(0,1)$. Under expected-cost minimisation, for which factors is reporting strictly preferable?
options: $\delta<\sqrt{3}/2$.
